The Magistrate's Sword
MAJ-ih-strayt SORD
noun phrase (theology / ethics)
From magistrate (Latin magister, a master, ruler) + sword; the coercive authority God grants the civil ruler in Romans 13:4.

📖 Biblical Definition

The magistrate's sword is the Scripture's name for the coercive authority God has given to the civil ruler — the lawful power to punish evildoers, even unto death. Paul sets it forth in Romans 13: the ruler is the minister of God, "for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil" (Rom 13:4). The sword is no human invention but a divine ordinance: God has appointed the magistrate to bear it for the restraint of wickedness and the protection of the good, so that the world is not given over to violence and anarchy. This is the ground of lawful government, lawful policing, just war, and capital justice. The same God who forbade private murder in the Sixth Commandment armed the public magistrate to execute the murderer (Gen 9:6), and the two stand together without contradiction: vengeance belongs to God, who has delegated a measure of it to the ordained magistrate, while forbidding it to the private hand (Rom 12:19). The magistrate's sword is to be used justly, under God, for the punishment of evil and the praise of good (1 Pet 2:14). This dictionary confesses the civil sword as a God-ordained authority, rejecting both the anarchism that denies it and the tyranny that abuses it.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Scripture's name for the coercive authority God grants the civil ruler — the lawful power to punish evildoers, even unto death (Rom 13:4). A divine ordinance for the restraint of wickedness and protection of the good, to be used justly under God, rejecting both anarchism and tyranny.

THE MAGISTRATE'S SWORD, noun phrase. The coercive authority God grants the civil ruler (Rom 13:4).

The ruler is the minister of God, who "beareth not the sword in vain."

A divine ordinance for the restraint of wickedness and the protection of the good.

The ground of lawful government, just war, and capital justice (Gen 9:6).

To be used justly under God; private vengeance is forbidden (Rom 12:19).

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 13:4 — "for he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil."

Gen 9:6 — "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man."

1 Pet 2:14 — "Or unto governors, as unto them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well."

Rom 12:19 — "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The magistrate's sword is corrupted by the anarchist and pacifist who deny the ruler any God-given power of coercion, and by the tyrant who wields it not for the punishment of evil and praise of good but for his own oppression — both forgetting that the sword is God's ordinance, held in trust and accountable to Him.

expand to see more

The first corruption denies the sword altogether: the pacifist who reads "resist not evil" (a word to the private man about personal retaliation) as binding the magistrate to bear no sword, and the anarchist who would abolish coercive authority entirely. But Paul calls the sword-bearing ruler the minister of God (Rom 13:4); to deny the sword is to deny the ordinance that restrains a fallen world from devouring itself. The dictionary names the magistrate's coercive authority as God-given and good.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but the opposite corruption is older and bloodier: the tyrant who bears the sword not as God's minister for good but for his own glory and oppression, punishing the righteous and praising the wicked. The sword is held in trust. The principle to recover is the whole biblical teaching: the magistrate's sword is a divine ordinance (Rom 13:4), to be used justly for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good (1 Pet 2:14), under God and accountable to Him — never to be abolished by the anarchist, never to be absolutized by the tyrant.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin magister (a ruler) + sword; the God-ordained coercive authority of the civil ruler to punish evil (Rom 13:4).
